title: Grade 6
emphasis: Reasoning, word parts, and shades of meaning

words.definition: able to be understood in more than one way, so the meaning is unclear

hero.text: Pixel's message said, "Meet at the tower," but it was ambiguous, because the city has two towers.

words.everyday: The sign "Fine for parking here" was ambiguous: did it mean parking was allowed, or that you would pay a fine?

contrast.nonExample: The recipe said, "Bake at 180 degrees for exactly 20 minutes."
contrast.explanation: That instruction has only one possible meaning, so it is clear, not ambiguous. Something ambiguous could honestly be read two or more ways.

items.prompt: What does "ambiguous" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The quiz question was ambiguous, so half the class answered it one way and half answered it another way.

options.text: having more than one possible meaning

items.hint: Why would two groups give two different answers to the same question?
items.explanation: Ambiguous means it can be understood in more than one way. Half the class read the question one way and half read it another way. A hard question is not the same thing: it can have one clear meaning and still be hard.

items.prompt: The prefix ambi- means "both" or "two ways," as in ambidextrous (able to use both hands well). Using that clue, what makes a sentence ambiguous?

options.text: It has two subjects in it
It was written by two people
It is twice as long as normal
It can be read in two or more ways

items.hint: Think about meaning that goes "two ways."
items.explanation: Ambi- means both or two ways. An ambiguous sentence points two ways at once: a reader could take its meaning in more than one direction. The number of subjects, writers, or words does not matter.

items.prompt: Is this headline ambiguous?
items.passage: A newspaper headline reads: "Students Help Dog Bite Victim." Readers can't tell if the students helped a person who was bitten or helped a dog bite someone.
items.hint: Can the headline be read in more than one way?
items.explanation: Yes. The headline has two possible meanings, and the reader can't tell which one is meant. That is exactly what ambiguous means.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the directions?
items.passage: Mr. Ortiz said, "Meet me by the big room after lunch." The school has a big gym and a big library, so some students went to one and some went to the other.
items.clue: a big gym and a big library
items.hint: The directions were not missing details. They pointed to two places at once.
items.explanation: "Big room" could mean two specific places, the gym or the library, so the directions were ambiguous. Vague means fuzzy or lacking detail in general; ambiguous means there are two (or more) clear possible readings. Nothing shows the directions were long or wrong.

items.prompt: What did the author do by leaving the ending ambiguous?
items.passage: In the novel's last chapter, the author never says whether the explorer survived. Some readers think she made it home; others think she was lost at sea. The author left the ending ambiguous on purpose.

options.text: Made the ending sad for every reader
Made the ending much shorter than the rest
Made the ending open to more than one reading
Explained exactly what happened to the explorer

items.hint: What do the two groups of readers think?
items.explanation: Some readers think she survived and others think she was lost, because the author never says. The ending is open to more than one reading, which is what ambiguous means. Explaining exactly what happened would make it clear, the opposite.

words.definition: clear and logical, with parts that connect and make sense together

hero.text: After the rescue, Kai gave a coherent report that explained each step in order.

words.everyday: Lily's essay was coherent because every paragraph connected back to her main idea.

contrast.nonExample: Max's story jumped from his dog to a volcano to his lunch, with no link between the parts.
contrast.explanation: The ideas do not connect, so the story is not coherent. In a coherent explanation, each part fits logically with the others.

items.prompt: Which explanation is coherent?
items.passage: Question: How does a puddle disappear on a sunny day?

options.text: Puddles, sunshine, my cousin likes ice cream, and clouds can be fluffy sometimes.
Water. Heat. Gone. It is the vapor thing, you know, with the sun and stuff.
The sun warms the water, the water turns into vapor, and the vapor rises into the air.

items.hint: Look for the answer whose parts connect in a logical order.
items.explanation: The coherent answer moves step by step: warming, then vapor, then rising. Each idea leads to the next. The other answers are jumbled or skip the connections, so they are hard to follow.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The witness was so shaken that her account was not ___; her sentences trailed off and her facts kept changing.
items.clue: sentences trailed off; facts kept changing
items.hint: What happens to an explanation when sentences trail off and facts keep changing?
items.explanation: "Sentences trailed off" and "facts kept changing" show that her account did not hold together logically. It was not coherent. Popular, private, and recent do not connect to those clues.

items.prompt: The prefix in- means "not." If a coherent speech is clear and logical, what is an incoherent speech?
items.hint: Put "not" in front of "clear and logical."
items.explanation: In- means not, so incoherent means not coherent: the ideas are jumbled and do not connect. A speech can be short, loud, or full of long words and still be perfectly coherent.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "coherent" in this sentence?
items.passage: Once Dev put his notes in order, his science presentation finally became coherent.
items.hint: What changed when Dev put his notes in order?
items.explanation: Putting notes in order made the ideas connect, so logical is the closest meaning. Coherent is about how well ideas fit together, not about color, length, or fame.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what coherent means.

chunks.text: The debate team's argument was coherent
had nothing to do with the others.

items.hint: A coherent argument has parts that connect. Which ending shows connection?
items.explanation: A coherent argument has reasons that link together, so "led clearly to the next" fits. Reasons that "had nothing to do with the others" would make the argument incoherent.

words.definition: to figure something out from clues and what you already know, even though it is not stated

hero.text: Juniper saw muddy footprints and an open window, so she inferred that someone had climbed inside.

words.everyday: From the dark clouds and the smell of rain, Omar inferred that a storm was coming.

contrast.nonExample: A sign on the door said "Closed on Mondays," so Tara knew the shop was closed.
contrast.explanation: Tara was told directly, so she didn't need to infer anything. To infer, you use clues to reach an idea that is not stated.

items.prompt: Does Ella infer something?
items.passage: Ella's friend walked in with a dripping umbrella and soaked shoes. Nobody mentioned the weather, but Ella decided it must be raining outside.
items.hint: Did anyone tell Ella it was raining?
items.explanation: Yes. Nobody said it was raining, but Ella used clues (the dripping umbrella and soaked shoes) to figure it out. That is inferring.

items.prompt: What does "infer" mean in this passage?
items.passage: The poem never names the season, but it mentions crunchy orange leaves and geese flying south. Readers can infer that the poem takes place in autumn.
items.hint: The poem never names the season. How do readers know it?
items.explanation: The season is never stated, so readers use clues like orange leaves and geese flying south to work it out. Infer means to reach an idea from clues.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: The scientist saw that the plant by the window grew taller than the one in the closet. From this evidence, she ___ that sunlight helps the plant grow.
items.hint: She SAW the height difference. What did she do with that evidence?
items.explanation: She observed (saw) the height difference, then used that evidence to infer an idea she could not see directly: sunlight helps growth. Guessed would mean she had no evidence, and ignored is the opposite of using it.

items.prompt: Which speaker uses "infer" correctly?

options.text: "I will infer the cake into the oven now."
"Nobody told me, but from your huge smile I infer that you passed."
"Please infer your name at the top of the page."
"The teacher inferred us a long story about Rome."

items.hint: Infer is about figuring something out. Which speaker is reasoning from a clue?
items.explanation: The speaker uses a clue (a huge smile) to figure out something unsaid (passing the test). That is inferring. The other lines confuse infer with put, write, or tell.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The note was unsigned, but because it mentioned the secret clubhouse, Mia could ___ that one of her three friends wrote it.
items.clue: unsigned; because it mentioned the secret clubhouse
items.hint: The note was unsigned. What did the clubhouse clue let Mia do?
items.explanation: Nobody signed the note, so Mia used a clue (only her friends knew about the clubhouse) to work out who wrote it. That is inferring. Announcing, forgetting, or denying would not use the clue.

words.definition: a particular way of seeing or thinking about something, shaped by where you are or what you have experienced

hero.text: From Bolt's perspective high in the sky, the traffic jam looked like a line of toy cars.

words.everyday: The story about the flood is told from the perspective of a young farmer.

contrast.nonExample: The thermometer showed 22 degrees.
contrast.explanation: A temperature reading is a fact, not a way of seeing things. A perspective is one person's point of view, which could differ from someone else's.

items.prompt: What does "perspective" mean in this passage?
items.passage: The history book shows the battle from the perspective of a soldier, while the diary shows it from the perspective of a nurse.
items.hint: The same battle is shown two ways. What changes from the soldier to the nurse?
items.explanation: The battle is the same, but the soldier and the nurse see it differently. Each one gives a point of view, which is a perspective.

items.prompt: The root spect means "look," as in spectator and inspect. How does that root help explain perspective?

options.text: It is a sound you can hear
It is a rule that must be followed
It is a way of looking at something

items.hint: Spect = look.
items.explanation: Spect means look, and a perspective is a way of looking at something, either with your eyes (the view from a hill) or with your mind (a viewpoint on an issue).

items.prompt: Does this show two different perspectives?
items.passage: Two students describe the same school play. Aria, who acted in it, says it was nerve-racking. Ben, who watched from the audience, says it was relaxing.
items.hint: Is it the same event seen in different ways?
items.explanation: Yes. Aria and Ben describe the same play differently because of where they were and what they did. Each one has a different perspective.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: After volunteering at the animal shelter, Jayden gained a new ___ on why pets need responsible owners.
items.hint: Volunteering changed how Jayden thinks about something. What did he gain?
items.explanation: Working at the shelter changed the way Jayden sees the issue. He gained a new perspective, a new way of thinking about it. The other words do not describe a viewpoint.

items.prompt: Which line uses "perspective" naturally?

options.text: "Can you perspective the window open for me?"
"My perspective broke when I dropped it on the floor."
"From a farmer's perspective, a week of rain is great news."
"The perspective arrived at noon on the yellow bus."

items.hint: A perspective belongs to someone and is a way of seeing things.
items.explanation: A farmer sees rain differently from someone planning a picnic. The first line names whose viewpoint it is. The other lines treat perspective as an action or an object.

words.definition: to publicly support or speak up for a cause, idea, or person

hero.text: Rex advocated for a safety net under the training tower, explaining the idea at every academy meeting.

words.everyday: The students advocated for more bike racks by writing letters to the city council.

contrast.nonExample: Nora agreed with the plan for a school garden, but she never said anything about it to anyone.
contrast.explanation: Privately agreeing is not advocating. To advocate, you speak or act openly to support something.

items.prompt: Which person advocates for something?

options.text: Leah tosses her can in the trash without thinking.
Leah forgets to go to the recycling meeting.
Leah gives a speech urging the school to start recycling.
Leah asks her friend what recycling means.

items.hint: Look for someone publicly speaking up in support of an idea.
items.explanation: Leah gives a speech urging the school to act, which is publicly supporting a cause. That is advocating. The other choices show no support or speaking up.

items.prompt: The root voc means "voice" or "call," as in vocal and vocabulary. Why does advocate contain this root?

options.text: Advocating means using your voice to support something
Advocating means singing in a loud choir
Advocating means staying quiet about a problem
Advocating means calling someone on the phone

items.hint: Think of what you do with your voice when you support an idea.
items.explanation: To advocate is to use your voice for a cause: speaking, writing, or arguing in favor of it. Staying quiet is the opposite, and singing or phone calls are not what the word means.

items.prompt: Which word is the OPPOSITE of "advocated" in this sentence?
items.passage: The scientist advocated for protecting the wetlands from new construction.
items.hint: If advocating means supporting, what is the opposite?
items.explanation: Advocated means openly supported, so opposed (argued against) is the opposite. Studying, visiting, or describing the wetlands does not show support or opposition.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Marisol didn't just like the idea of a school garden; she ___ for it at every assembly and collected 200 signatures.
items.clue: didn't just like; at every assembly; 200 signatures
items.hint: "Didn't just like" tells you she did something stronger. What did she do in public?
items.explanation: Hoping and wishing happen quietly in your head. Marisol spoke at assemblies and gathered signatures, which is strong, public support. Advocated fits that degree of action.

items.prompt: Is Darius advocating?
items.passage: Darius is asked to vote on whether the library should open on weekends. He has no opinion, so he flips a coin to decide.
items.hint: Is Darius speaking up for an idea he supports?
items.explanation: No. Darius has no opinion and does not speak up for anything. Advocating means actively and publicly supporting a cause.

words.definition: to set aside or give out something, such as money, time, or space, for a particular purpose

hero.text: Nova allocated one hour of training to flying and one hour to first aid.

words.everyday: The town allocated part of its budget to repairing the playground.

contrast.nonExample: Leo spent his allowance on whatever caught his eye at the store, with no plan at all.
contrast.explanation: Spending without a plan is not allocating. To allocate is to decide ahead of time how to divide something up for specific purposes.

items.prompt: What does "allocated" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The class allocated ten minutes for each group's presentation.
items.hint: Each group got a certain amount of time. Who decided, and how?
items.explanation: The class decided how to divide the time and gave each group ten minutes. To allocate is to set aside a share for a purpose.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Because the art club had only twenty brushes, Ms. Kim had to ___ them carefully so every table got some.
items.clue: only twenty brushes; so every table got some
items.hint: There were only twenty brushes. What did Ms. Kim need to do so every table got some?
items.explanation: "Only twenty brushes" and "so every table got some" show a limited supply that had to be divided fairly. That is allocating.

items.prompt: Is this an example of allocating?
items.passage: A city council decides to spend $50,000 of its budget on new streetlights and $20,000 on park benches.
items.hint: Is the council deciding how to divide its money for specific purposes?
items.explanation: Yes. The council divides its money and assigns each part to a specific purpose. That is allocating.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Before the fundraiser even started, the student council met to ___ the money they hoped to raise: half for the field trip and half for new library books.
items.clue: Before the fundraiser even started; half for... half for
items.hint: The money has not been raised yet. What can you do with money you plan to get?
items.explanation: The money was not collected yet, so it could not be spent, donated, or counted. The council was planning how to divide it ahead of time, which is allocating.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what allocate means.
items.hint: Allocating means setting something aside for a purpose.
items.explanation: Allocating gives a share of something to a specific purpose, so "to passing drills" fits. "Without any plan or purpose" contradicts the meaning of allocate.

words.definition: with a name that is unknown or not given

hero.text: An anonymous note thanked Pixel for fixing the school's power, but nobody signed it.

words.everyday: An anonymous donor gave the hospital money for a new children's wing.

contrast.nonExample: Grace signed her full name in big letters at the bottom of her poem.
contrast.explanation: Grace's name is clearly shown, so the poem is not anonymous. Anonymous means the name is hidden or unknown.

items.prompt: Is this survey anonymous?
items.passage: A survey asks students for their opinions about school lunch and tells them NOT to write their names.
items.hint: Will anyone know who gave each answer?
items.explanation: Yes. No names are written, so no one knows who gave each answer. That makes the survey anonymous.

items.prompt: The prefix an- means "without," and the root onym means "name," as in synonym. So an anonymous letter is...

options.text: a letter that is very old

items.hint: An- = without. Onym = name.
items.explanation: Put the parts together: without + name. An anonymous letter has no name on it, so the writer is unknown. Being old or in code is a different idea.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: No one knows who composed the old folk song, so the concert program listed its composer as ___.
items.hint: No one knows who wrote it. How do you describe an author whose name is unknown?
items.explanation: "No one knows who composed" the song is the clue: the composer's name is unknown, so the composer is anonymous.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "anonymous" in this sentence?
items.passage: An anonymous caller gave the police a tip about the missing painting.
items.hint: What do the police NOT know about the caller?
items.explanation: The police do not know the caller's name, so unnamed is closest. The caller might also be nervous or honest, but anonymous only tells you the name is unknown.

items.prompt: Which line uses "anonymous" correctly?

options.text: "I left an anonymous compliment in the kindness box. Nobody will know it was me."
"My anonymous name is Jordan, and I live on Elm Street."
"The puppy was so anonymous that it barked all night long."
"Write your anonymous answer in pen, then sign your name below."

items.hint: Anonymous means the name is hidden.
items.explanation: The first speaker hides their identity: "Nobody will know it was me." The other lines give a name, describe barking, or ask for a signature, which contradicts anonymous.

words.definition: something you believe is true without having proof

hero.text: Bolt made the assumption that the alarm was just a drill, but Juniper checked and found a real problem.

words.everyday: Her assumption that the test would be easy turned out to be wrong.

contrast.nonExample: Ravi measured the table with a tape measure and found it was exactly two meters long.
contrast.explanation: A measurement has been checked, so it is not an assumption. An assumption is accepted as true without checking or proof.

items.prompt: What does "assumption" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Ken's assumption that the store would be open on Sunday left him standing in front of a locked door.
items.hint: Did Ken check the store hours?
items.explanation: Ken believed the store would be open but never checked, and he was wrong. A belief you accept without proof is an assumption.

items.prompt: Is Ana making an assumption?
items.passage: Without ever talking to him, Ana decides that her new classmate doesn't like music because he is quiet.
items.hint: Does Ana have any proof?
items.explanation: Yes. Ana has no evidence. She has never talked to him about music. She believes it anyway, which is an assumption.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Without checking the weather report, Kim made the ___ that it would be sunny and left her umbrella at home.
items.hint: Kim did not check anything. Which word means believing without evidence?
items.explanation: A conclusion is reached by reasoning from evidence, and an observation comes from looking carefully. Kim checked nothing, so her belief was an assumption.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Good scientists test every ___ in an experiment, because an idea that seems obvious can still be wrong.
items.clue: an idea that seems obvious can still be wrong
items.hint: What kind of idea "seems obvious" but still needs testing?
items.explanation: "An idea that seems obvious can still be wrong" describes an assumption: something we believe without proof. Scientists test assumptions instead of trusting them.

items.prompt: Why does the passage call the historians' belief an assumption?
items.passage: For years, historians believed an old map was drawn by a famous explorer. No one had ever tested it. Then ink tests showed the map was made 100 years after his death. Their belief had been an assumption.

options.text: The ink tests proved it was true
The explorer had said so himself
It was written right on the map

items.clue: No one had ever tested it
items.hint: Look for the sentence about testing.
items.explanation: "No one had ever tested it" shows the historians believed it without proof. That is an assumption. The ink tests actually proved the belief wrong.

words.definition: an unfair leaning for or against someone or something that affects judgment

hero.text: Kai noticed his own bias: he always picked his best friend for missions, even when someone else was better suited.

words.everyday: The judge stepped down from the baking contest because her son had entered and she worried about bias.

contrast.nonExample: The coach chose the relay team by timing everyone in the same race and picking the four fastest runners.
contrast.explanation: Using the same test for everyone is fair, so there is no bias. Bias means unfairly favoring or opposing someone.

items.prompt: Does this referee show bias?
items.passage: A referee calls fouls on only one team, even when players on both teams break the same rules.
items.hint: Is the referee treating both teams the same way?
items.explanation: Yes. Both teams break the same rules, but only one is punished. That unfair leaning against one team is bias.

items.prompt: What does "bias" mean in this passage?
items.passage: The article showed bias: it called one candidate's ideas "brilliant" and called the other candidate's identical ideas "silly."

options.text: an unfair leaning toward one side

items.hint: The ideas were identical. Were they described the same way?
items.explanation: Identical ideas were praised for one candidate and mocked for the other. That unfair leaning toward one side is bias, the opposite of a balanced summary.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "bias" in this sentence?
items.passage: Ms. Diaz graded the essays with the students' names covered to avoid bias.
items.hint: Why would covering names help? What was she trying to keep?
items.explanation: Covering names keeps Ms. Diaz from favoring anyone, so she grades with fairness, the opposite of bias. Opinion is not the opposite: everyone has opinions, but bias is when a leaning makes judgment unfair.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Because the survey only asked people who already loved the park, its results showed clear ___ in favor of keeping it open.
items.clue: only asked people who already loved the park
items.hint: Only one kind of person was asked. What does that do to the results?
items.explanation: Asking only people who already loved the park tilts the results toward one side. That unfair leaning is bias.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the problem?
items.passage: When scoring science fair projects, one judge secretly gave extra points to every project from her own school.
items.hint: Was this on purpose? Was it fair?
items.explanation: Everyone has opinions, but the judge let her loyalty unfairly change the scores. That is bias. It was not an accident, because she did it on purpose.

words.definition: to work together with others to make or achieve something

hero.text: Pixel and Rex collaborated on a new rescue drone: Pixel wrote the code and Rex built the frame.

words.everyday: Two authors collaborated on the picture book; one wrote the words and the other painted the art.

contrast.nonExample: Each student built a volcano model alone at home and brought it in on Monday.
contrast.explanation: Working separately is not collaborating. To collaborate, people work together toward one shared goal.

items.prompt: Which group is collaborating?

options.text: Three classmates each write their own separate report.
Three classmates argue and then quit the project.
Three classmates read quietly by themselves.
Three classmates each write one part of a shared report.

items.hint: Look for people working together on ONE shared project.
items.explanation: Writing parts of one shared report means working together toward a common goal. That is collaborating. Writing separate reports or reading alone is working by yourself.

items.prompt: The prefix col- means "together," and the root labor means "work." What does collaborate mean?
items.hint: Col- = together. Labor = work.
items.explanation: Together + work = collaborate. The word is built from its meaning: working together with others.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Scientists from fifteen countries ___ to build the International Space Station, sharing designs, parts, and astronauts.
items.hint: The countries were sharing. Were they working against each other or together?
items.explanation: "Sharing designs, parts, and astronauts" shows the countries worked together toward one goal. Competed would mean they worked against each other.

items.prompt: Are the bakeries collaborating?
items.passage: Two rival bakeries each try to bake the biggest cake in town so they can win the contest prize.
items.hint: Are they working together or against each other?
items.explanation: No. The bakeries are competing against each other, not working together. Collaborating means sharing the work toward one shared goal.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what collaborate means.

chunks.text: without ever talking to one another.
each adding a verse or a melody.

items.hint: Collaborating means working together. Which ending shows teamwork?
items.explanation: Each member contributing to one song shows teamwork, so "each adding a verse or a melody" fits. Never talking to one another is the opposite of collaborating.

words.definition: able to work, fit, or exist together without problems

hero.text: Pixel checked that the new battery was compatible with Bolt's suit before plugging it in.

words.everyday: The new game is compatible with older tablets, so Amir can still play it.

contrast.nonExample: Two roommates argue every day about noise, mess, and what time to turn off the lights.
contrast.explanation: They cannot live together smoothly, so they are not compatible. Compatible things or people work well together.

items.prompt: Are these headphones compatible with the music player?
items.passage: Lena's new headphones plug right into her old music player and work perfectly.
items.hint: Do the two things work together without problems?
items.explanation: Yes. The headphones and the player work together with no trouble, so they are compatible.

items.prompt: The suffix -ible means "able to be," and the prefix in- means "not." What does incompatible mean?
items.hint: In- = not. Compatible = able to work together.
items.explanation: In- (not) + compatible (able to work together) = not able to work together. Being breakable or too large is a different idea.

items.prompt: What does "compatible" mean in this passage?
items.passage: The two plans for the class party were not compatible: one moved the party to Friday, and the other cancelled all Friday events.

options.text: able to fit together without conflict

items.hint: Could both plans happen at once?
items.explanation: One plan puts the party on Friday and the other cancels Friday events, so both cannot happen. They clash, which means they are not compatible.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Before a blood transfusion, doctors test whether the donor's blood type is ___ with the patient's blood.
items.hint: The doctors need to know if the two blood types can safely mix.
items.explanation: Doctors test whether the blood types can safely work together in one body. Compatible means able to exist together without problems.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Jada and Theo have different hobbies, but they split chores fairly and rarely argue, so they are great roommates. They are ___.
items.clue: split chores fairly and rarely argue
items.hint: They are different, yet they live together well.
items.explanation: Identical would mean exactly the same, but they have different hobbies. They still live together smoothly, which is what compatible means.

words.definition: including all or nearly all of the important parts; complete

hero.text: Juniper made a comprehensive map of the city that showed every street, park, and hidden tunnel.

words.everyday: The museum guide gives a comprehensive history of the dinosaurs, from the first ones to the last.

contrast.nonExample: Owen's book report described only the first chapter of the novel.
contrast.explanation: Covering only one chapter is partial, not comprehensive. Something comprehensive covers everything important.

items.prompt: What does "comprehensive" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The doctor gave Sam a comprehensive checkup, testing his eyes, ears, heart, lungs, and reflexes.
items.clue: eyes, ears, heart, lungs, and reflexes
items.hint: Look at the long list of things the doctor checked.
items.explanation: The doctor checked eyes, ears, heart, lungs, and reflexes, which is nearly everything important. That makes the checkup comprehensive.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The study guide was ___: it reviewed every single topic from all six units.
items.clue: every single topic from all six units
items.hint: What word describes something that covers EVERY topic?
items.explanation: "Every single topic from all six units" is the clue. A guide that covers everything is comprehensive. Brief means short, which points the other way.

items.prompt: Which description best fits Ava's report?
items.passage: Ava's report on the Civil War was twenty pages long, but it discussed only one cause of the war and skipped all the others.
items.hint: Length and coverage are different things.
items.explanation: Twenty pages is long, but skipping most causes means the report is not complete. Comprehensive is about covering all the important parts, not about how many pages there are.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "comprehensive" in this sentence?
items.passage: The company did a comprehensive search for the lost files, checking every computer in the building.
items.hint: If comprehensive means covering everything, what means covering only some?
items.explanation: A comprehensive search checks everything, and a partial search checks only some places. A search can be careful or expensive and still not be complete.

items.prompt: Is this field guide comprehensive?
items.passage: A field guide claims to cover "the birds of our state," but it describes only the 10 most common birds, even though more than 400 kinds live there.
items.hint: How much of the topic does the guide leave out?
items.explanation: No. Ten birds out of more than 400 leaves out almost everything, so the guide is partial, not comprehensive. A comprehensive guide would include all or nearly all of them.

words.definition: saying what is needed clearly, in just a few words

hero.text: Instead of a long speech, Rex gave a concise warning: "Bridge cracked. Use the tunnel."

words.everyday: A good summary is concise; it gives the main idea without extra details.

contrast.nonExample: When asked "What time is it?" Tim talked for five minutes, including a long story about where he bought his watch.
contrast.explanation: Using far more words than needed is wordy, the opposite of concise. A concise answer is short and still clear.

items.prompt: Which answer is the most concise?
items.passage: Question: Why did the classroom plant die?

options.text: Well, so, there was this plant, and I think maybe it kind of needed some water, I guess.
Plants are living things that grow.
I don't really know, but plants are cool.

items.hint: Look for the answer that is short AND actually answers the question.
items.explanation: "It didn't get enough water" answers the question clearly in a few words. The rambling answer is wordy, and the others are short but do not answer the question, so they are not useful.

items.prompt: Which word best describes this headline?
items.passage: Headline: "Snowstorm Closes All City Schools Tuesday"
items.hint: Is the headline short? Is it clear about what, where, and when?
items.explanation: The headline is short, and it still tells what (schools close), why (snowstorm), and when (Tuesday). That is concise. Vague would mean short but missing key information.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Ms. Patel asked for ___ answers of one or two sentences, with no extra filler.
items.clue: one or two sentences, with no extra filler
items.hint: "One or two sentences" and "no extra filler" describe what kind of answer?
items.explanation: Answers of one or two sentences with no filler are short and to the point, which is concise. Detailed answers would usually be longer.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "concise" in this sentence?
items.passage: The editor helped turn the rambling article into a concise one.
items.hint: The article started out "rambling." That is a clue to the opposite.
items.explanation: Rambling writing uses too many words, so wordy is the opposite of concise. A piece can be clear or accurate and still be concise, so those are not opposites.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what concise means.
items.hint: Concise means short and clear.
items.explanation: Three clear sentences is short and to the point, which is concise. Twelve rambling pages is wordy, the opposite.

words.definition: the standards or rules used to judge or decide something (singular: criterion)

hero.text: The academy listed three criteria for new heroes: courage, kindness, and teamwork.

words.everyday: The science fair judges used criteria such as creativity, accuracy, and a clear presentation.

contrast.nonExample: Zara closed her eyes and grabbed any book off the library shelf.
contrast.explanation: Zara used no standards to choose, so there were no criteria. Criteria are the rules or standards used to make a decision.

items.prompt: What does "criteria" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The criteria for the poster contest were neatness, originality, and a clear message.
items.hint: Neatness, originality, and a clear message are things the judges look FOR.
items.explanation: Neatness, originality, and a clear message are the standards the posters will be judged by. Those are criteria.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: To join the robotics team, students had to meet two ___: passing grades and perfect attendance at practice.
items.hint: Passing grades and perfect attendance are rules you must meet to be chosen.
items.explanation: The two requirements a student must meet to join are criteria. You "meet criteria"; rewards come after, and obstacles get in the way.

items.prompt: Are these criteria?
items.passage: The class agrees that its field trip must cost under $10 per student, be within an hour's drive, and relate to science.
items.hint: Are these standards the class will use to decide?
items.explanation: Yes. Cost, distance, and topic are standards the class will use to judge each trip idea. Those are criteria.

items.prompt: What were the criteria?
items.passage: When choosing a new class pet, the students agreed it had to be quiet, cheap to feed, and safe to hold. A hamster met all three criteria; a parrot met none.

options.text: being quiet, cheap to feed, and safe to hold

items.clue: had to be quiet, cheap to feed, and safe to hold
items.hint: Criteria are the standards, not the choices being judged.
items.explanation: The standards were being quiet, cheap to feed, and safe to hold. The hamster and the parrot were the options judged BY those criteria.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "criteria" in this sentence?
items.passage: The city set strict criteria for which old buildings could be called "historic."
items.hint: What would a city use to decide if a building counts as historic?
items.explanation: The city decides using rules or standards that a building must meet, such as its age. Standards is the closest meaning.

words.definition: to reach an answer by careful reasoning from facts or evidence

hero.text: Juniper deduced that the thief was left-handed from the way the lock had been scratched.

words.everyday: From the fossil's sharp, pointed teeth, scientists deduced that the animal ate meat.

contrast.nonExample: Ollie picked answer C without even reading the question.
contrast.explanation: Choosing at random is guessing. To deduce, you reason step by step from evidence.

items.prompt: Did Mom deduce something?
items.passage: All the cookies were gone, a trail of crumbs led to the dog bed, and only the dog had been home. Mom decided the dog ate them.
items.hint: Did Mom use evidence to reason it out?
items.explanation: Yes. Mom put together facts (empty plate, crumb trail, only the dog home) to reach an answer. That is deducing.

items.prompt: The prefix de- can mean "from," and the root duc means "lead," as in conduct. So when you deduce something, you...

options.text: lead a group on a trip
take a number away from a total
let the evidence lead you to an answer

items.hint: De- = from. Duc = lead.
items.explanation: When you deduce, the facts lead you from evidence to an answer. Taking a number away is "deduct," a different word, and guessing skips the evidence.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Everyone who ate the potato salad got sick, and no one who skipped it did. Using these facts, the health inspector ___ that the salad caused the illness.
items.hint: The inspector used facts. Which word means reasoning from evidence?
items.explanation: Guessing and assuming happen without evidence, and imagining is make-believe. The inspector reasoned carefully from facts, so deduced is the best fit.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: A good detective can ___ a lot about a person from small clues like muddy boots or ink-stained fingers.
items.hint: What does a detective DO with small clues?
items.explanation: Detectives use small clues to reason their way to answers about a person. That is deducing. The other de- words look similar but mean very different things.

items.prompt: What does "deduced" mean in this passage?
items.passage: Ancient sailors noticed that ships disappeared bottom-first over the horizon. From this, they deduced that the Earth's surface must be curved.

options.text: figured out by reasoning from what they saw

items.hint: "From this" points back to the evidence.
items.explanation: The sailors noticed something (ships vanishing bottom-first) and reasoned from it to an answer (Earth is curved). Deduced means figured out by reasoning from evidence.

words.definition: to become or make smaller, weaker, or less

hero.text: As Kai calmly explained the plan, the crowd's panic began to diminish.

words.everyday: The sound of the train diminished as it moved farther away.

contrast.nonExample: The snowball grew bigger and bigger as it rolled down the hill.
contrast.explanation: Growing is the opposite of diminishing. To diminish is to get smaller or weaker.

items.prompt: What does "diminished" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The pain in Ella's ankle diminished after she rested it for a week.
items.hint: What usually happens to pain after rest?
items.explanation: After a week of rest, the pain got smaller. Diminished means became less.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "diminished" in this sentence?
items.passage: Over the dry summer, the water in the pond diminished until only mud was left.
items.hint: Diminished means got smaller. Which word means got bigger?
items.explanation: Diminished means got less, so increased is the opposite. Shrank means nearly the same as diminished, and evaporated is how the water got less.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: The noise from the party ___ as the guests left, but a few people were still laughing in the kitchen.
items.clue: a few people were still laughing
items.hint: Was the noise completely gone?
items.explanation: Vanished means gone completely, but "a few people were still laughing," so some noise remained. The noise got smaller, which is diminished.

items.prompt: Is this an example of diminishing?
items.passage: All afternoon, more and more fans poured into the stadium, and the cheering grew louder and louder.
items.hint: Is something getting smaller or weaker?
items.explanation: No. The crowd and the cheering are both growing, which is the opposite of diminishing. Diminish means to become smaller, weaker, or less.

items.prompt: Diminish shares the root mini, meaning "small," with miniature and minimum. Which sentence uses diminish correctly?

options.text: The balloon diminished to twice its first size.
The crowd diminished from 50 people to 500.
Her excitement diminished into total joy.
The candle's light diminished as it burned down.

items.hint: Mini = small. Diminish should mean getting smaller.
items.explanation: The candle's light getting weaker is a true example of diminishing. A balloon doubling, a crowd growing to 500, and excitement turning into joy are all increases.

words.definition: most powerful, important, or noticeable; in control over others

hero.text: Blue is the dominant color in Nova's new suit, with only thin silver stripes.

words.everyday: In the forest, oak trees were the dominant species, far outnumbering the pines.

contrast.nonExample: In the painting, a tiny red dot sits in one corner of a huge green field.
contrast.explanation: The tiny red dot is a minor detail. Green is the dominant color because it fills most of the space and catches the eye.

items.prompt: What does "dominant" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Wolves in a pack follow the dominant pair, who lead the hunts and eat first.
items.clue: lead the hunts and eat first
items.hint: Who leads and eats first?
items.explanation: The pair that leads the hunts and eats first has the most power in the pack. That is dominant.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Rain was the ___ feature of the region's weather, falling on almost 300 days each year.
items.hint: Almost 300 days a year! Is rain a small part or the main part of the weather?
items.explanation: Rain on almost 300 days a year makes it the main, most noticeable feature. Dominant fits; rare is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Most people write, throw, and eat with the same hand. That hand is called their ___ hand.
items.hint: Which hand is the strongest and most used?
items.explanation: The hand you use most is your dominant hand, the one in charge. Bossy describes a personality, and superior means better than others, which is not what we mean about hands.

items.prompt: Is there a dominant member in this group?
items.passage: In a group project, all four students share the work equally and take turns leading the meetings.
items.hint: Does one person have more power or control?
items.explanation: No. Everyone shares the work and the leading equally, so no one is dominant. Dominant means having the most power or control.

items.prompt: Which line uses "dominant" naturally?

options.text: "Hip-hop was the dominant sound at the festival; almost every stage played it."
"I will dominant the dishes after dinner tonight."
"The tiny stain was so dominant that nobody could see it."
"She whispered in a dominant voice that no one could hear."

items.hint: Dominant means most powerful or noticeable.
items.explanation: Hip-hop played on almost every stage was the main, most noticeable sound. That is dominant. A stain nobody sees or a voice nobody hears is the opposite.

words.definition: the ability to understand and share the feelings of another person

hero.text: Juniper showed empathy for the lost child, kneeling down and saying, "I would be scared too."

words.everyday: Because Malik once broke his arm, he had empathy for his friend who was wearing a cast.

contrast.nonExample: When Jen dropped her lunch tray, Chris laughed and walked away.
contrast.explanation: Chris ignored how Jen felt, so he showed no empathy. Empathy means imagining and understanding someone else's feelings.

items.prompt: Does Sofia show empathy?
items.passage: When Sofia's friend lost a big game, Sofia remembered how awful losing felt and sat with her quietly.
items.hint: Is Sofia understanding how her friend feels?
items.explanation: Yes. Sofia remembered a similar feeling and used it to understand her friend's sadness. That is empathy.

items.prompt: The root path means "feeling," as in sympathy. The prefix em- means "in." So empathy is...

options.text: feeling what is inside another person's heart

items.hint: Em- = in. Path = feeling.
items.explanation: Empathy means getting "into" someone else's feelings: understanding what they feel as if from the inside. The "path" here is about feeling, not a trail.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what Ana felt?
items.passage: Ana didn't just feel sorry for the new student. She imagined being in his shoes, not knowing anyone and getting lost in the halls, and she truly understood how lonely he felt.
items.clue: didn't just feel sorry; imagined being in his shoes
items.hint: "Didn't just feel sorry" tells you it was more than sympathy.
items.explanation: Sympathy and pity mean feeling sorry FOR someone. Ana went further: she imagined being in his place and understood his loneliness from the inside. That deeper understanding is empathy.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Good nurses need ___, because patients feel calmer when someone truly understands their fear.
items.hint: What helps someone understand another person's fear?
items.explanation: "Truly understands their fear" describes empathy, the ability to understand and share another person's feelings.

items.prompt: What changed in the main character?
items.passage: In the novel, Maya can't stand her grumpy neighbor at first. Then she learns that his family moved far away and he has been alone for years. Her anger turns to empathy.

options.text: She started to be afraid of the neighbor
She decided to move away too
She began to understand how the neighbor felt
She forgot all about the neighbor

items.hint: What did Maya learn, and how did it change her feelings?
items.explanation: Learning about his loneliness helped Maya understand his feelings. Her anger turned into empathy, the ability to understand someone else's feelings.

words.definition: to make something better, stronger, or more attractive

hero.text: Pixel enhanced the blurry security photo until the license plate was easy to read.

words.everyday: A pinch of salt can enhance the sweet flavor of caramel.

contrast.nonExample: Spilling juice on the poster smeared all the letters.
contrast.explanation: The spill made the poster worse, not better. To enhance is to improve something that already exists.

items.prompt: What does "enhanced" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The stage lights enhanced the dancers' costumes, making the colors glow.
items.hint: What did the lights do to the colors?
items.explanation: The lights made the colors glow, so the costumes looked even better. Enhanced means improved or made more striking.

items.prompt: Which word means the OPPOSITE of "enhance" in this sentence?
items.passage: Regular practice will enhance your piano skills.
items.hint: Enhance means make better. What means make worse?
items.explanation: Enhance means improve, so weaken is the opposite. Improve is a synonym, not an opposite.

items.prompt: Is the gardener enhancing her soil?
items.passage: A gardener mixes compost into her soil so her tomato plants grow healthier and produce more fruit.
items.hint: Is she making something better?
items.explanation: Yes. Adding compost improves the soil that is already there, so the plants grow better. That is enhancing.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: The museum didn't paint a new picture. It cleaned the old painting and added better lighting to ___ its colors.
items.hint: The painting already existed. What did the museum do to it?
items.explanation: Create and invent mean making something new, but the painting already existed. Cleaning and lighting improved what was there, which is enhancing. Disguise would hide the colors.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what enhance means.

chunks.text: by making the cells blurry and hard to see.
by making tiny cells look sharper.

items.hint: Enhance means make better.
items.explanation: Making cells look sharper improves the view, which is enhancing. Making them blurry would make the view worse.

words.definition: to judge carefully how good, useful, or important something is

hero.text: Rex evaluated each escape route, checking which was safest before leading everyone out.

words.everyday: The teacher evaluated each project using a checklist of what a strong report needs.

contrast.nonExample: Ivy copied facts from the first website she found without checking whether they were true.
contrast.explanation: Ivy never judged the source's quality, so she did not evaluate it. Evaluating means carefully weighing strengths and weaknesses.

items.prompt: Is Jamal evaluating?
items.passage: Before buying a bike, Jamal compares the price, weight, and reviews of three different models.
items.hint: Is Jamal carefully judging which is best?
items.explanation: Yes. Jamal weighs the strengths and weaknesses of each bike before deciding. That is evaluating.

items.prompt: Look inside the word evaluate: e-VALU-ate. Which word is hiding in it, and what does that suggest?

options.text: valley, so evaluate means walking down a hill
vacation, so evaluate means taking a break
violin, so evaluate means playing music
value, so evaluate means judging how valuable something is

items.hint: Find a smaller word inside e-VALU-ate.
items.explanation: Evaluate contains "value." To evaluate something is to figure out its value: how good, useful, or important it is.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Before trusting a news story, it is smart to ___ the source: Who wrote it, and what evidence do they give?
items.clue: Who wrote it, and what evidence do they give?
items.hint: The questions after the colon tell you what to do with the source.
items.explanation: Asking who wrote it and what evidence they give are ways of judging how trustworthy a source is. That is evaluating.

items.prompt: Describing a movie tells what happens in it. Which task asks you to EVALUATE the movie?

options.text: List the names of all the main characters in order.
Retell the plot from the beginning to the end.
Explain whether the ending worked, and why.
Draw a picture of the scene you remember best.

items.hint: Evaluating means judging quality.
items.explanation: Deciding whether the ending worked and explaining why is a judgment about quality. That is evaluating. Listing, retelling, and drawing describe the movie without judging it.

items.prompt: Which line uses "evaluate" correctly?

options.text: "I evaluated my sandwich into four equal pieces."
"The geese evaluated south for the winter months."
"Let's evaluate both plans and pick the one with fewer risks."
"Please evaluate the lights when you leave the room."

items.hint: Evaluate means carefully judge.
items.explanation: Comparing two plans to see which has fewer risks is careful judging, so the first line is correct. The others confuse evaluate with cut, fly, or turn off.

words.definition: a short part taken from a longer piece of writing, music, film, or speech

hero.text: At the ceremony, Kai read an excerpt from the academy's founding speech: just two powerful sentences.

words.everyday: The reading test included an excerpt from a novel, followed by questions about the main character.

contrast.nonExample: Julia read the entire novel, from the first page to the very last.
contrast.explanation: Reading the whole book is not reading an excerpt. An excerpt is only a short piece taken from something longer.

items.prompt: What does "excerpt" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Our textbook includes an excerpt from a famous speech given in 1963.

options.text: a short part taken from a longer work
a summary in your own words

items.hint: Does a textbook usually print the whole speech, or just a piece?
items.explanation: An excerpt is a short part taken from a longer work, word for word. It is not the complete speech, and it is not a summary in your own words.

items.prompt: The prefix ex- means "out," as in exit and export. So an excerpt is a piece that has been...

options.text: added to the end of a book
taken out of a longer work

items.hint: Ex- = out. What happens to the piece?
items.explanation: An excerpt is pulled out of a longer work so it can be shared or studied by itself. It is not added, and it is not left out.

items.prompt: Is this an excerpt?
items.passage: A movie trailer shows a few short scenes taken from a two-hour film.
items.hint: Are these short pieces taken from something longer?
items.explanation: Yes. The trailer uses short pieces taken directly from the longer film, so each clip is an excerpt.

items.prompt: Which of these is an EXCERPT from the story "Goldilocks and the Three Bears"?

options.text: A girl enters the bears' house, tries their things, and runs off.
"Someone's been eating my porridge!" cried Papa Bear.
This story teaches readers to respect other people's things.
Goldilocks is my favorite fairy tale of all time.

items.hint: An excerpt uses the exact words from the story itself.
items.explanation: An excerpt copies the author's actual words, like Papa Bear's line. A retelling of events is a summary, a lesson is a theme, and "my favorite" is an opinion.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The radio host played a 30-second ___ from the new symphony so listeners could hear its opening melody.
items.hint: A 30-second piece taken from a much longer symphony is called what?
items.explanation: A 30-second piece of a long symphony is a short part taken from a longer work: an excerpt.

words.definition: a possible explanation or prediction that can be tested (plural: hypotheses)

hero.text: Pixel's hypothesis was that the robot froze because its battery got too cold, so she tested it in a warm room.

words.everyday: Leah's hypothesis was that plants would grow faster with music, so she set up two groups to compare.

contrast.nonExample: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
contrast.explanation: That is a fact that has been tested many times, not a hypothesis. A hypothesis is an idea that still needs to be tested.

items.prompt: What does "hypothesis" mean in this passage?
items.passage: Before the experiment, the class wrote a hypothesis: "Ice will melt faster in salt water than in fresh water."

options.text: a prediction that can be tested

items.hint: It was written BEFORE the experiment.
items.explanation: The class wrote it before testing, as a prediction they could check. That is a hypothesis. The final result comes after the experiment.

items.prompt: Is Marco forming a hypothesis?
items.passage: Marco thinks his cat sleeps more on rainy days, so he plans to record her naps and the weather for a month.
items.hint: Does Marco have an idea that he plans to test?
items.explanation: Yes. Marco has a possible explanation (rain makes the cat sleep more) and a plan to test it. That is a hypothesis.

items.prompt: Which statement is a hypothesis?

options.text: Bean plants are the prettiest plants in the garden.
If we add fertilizer, the bean plants will grow taller.
The bean plants grew five centimeters in two weeks.
We used three pots, soil, and a packet of bean seeds.

items.hint: A hypothesis is a prediction you can test. It is not an opinion, a result, or a list of materials.
items.explanation: The fertilizer statement predicts something that an experiment could test. "Prettiest" is an opinion, "grew five centimeters" is a result, and the last choice lists materials.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The scientists' ___ turned out to be wrong, but testing it still taught them something new about the virus.
items.clue: turned out to be wrong; testing it
items.hint: What kind of idea can be tested and turn out to be wrong?
items.explanation: "Testing it" and "turned out to be wrong" fit a hypothesis: an idea that is tested and may or may not be right.

items.prompt: The prefix hypo- means "under," and thesis means "idea" or "proposal." Why is hypothesis a good name for an idea that has not been proven yet?

options.text: It is an idea buried under the ground
It is an idea placed under an experiment, to be tested
It is an idea proven many times already
It is an idea too small to matter

items.hint: Hypo- = under. Think about what supports or sits beneath an experiment.
items.explanation: A hypothesis is the starting idea that an experiment is built on and tests. It is not proven yet. Once it has been tested many times, it is no longer just a hypothesis.

words.definition: something that encourages a person to do something, such as a reward

hero.text: As an incentive to finish training early, Bolt promised the cadets a flight through the clouds.

words.everyday: The store offered a free smoothie as an incentive for customers to bring reusable bags.

contrast.nonExample: Sara cleaned her room on a Saturday. Nobody asked her or offered her anything for it.
contrast.explanation: Nothing was offered to encourage her, so there was no incentive. An incentive is something offered to push someone to act.

items.prompt: What does "incentive" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The library offered stickers as an incentive for kids to read twenty books over the summer.
items.hint: Why does the library offer stickers?
items.explanation: The stickers encourage kids to read more. Something offered to encourage an action is an incentive, not a rule or a punishment.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Free parking was the main ___ that convinced shoppers to try the new market.
items.hint: Something "convinced" shoppers to come. Was it helpful or a problem?
items.explanation: Free parking encouraged shoppers to come, so it was an incentive. An obstacle would keep them away.

items.prompt: Which of these is an incentive to recycle?

options.text: Paying a fee for every bag of trash you throw out
A poster that lists what can be recycled
Getting 10 cents back for every can you return
A new law that bans plastic grocery bags

items.hint: An incentive is a reward that makes you WANT to do something.
items.explanation: Getting money back rewards recycling, so it is an incentive. A fee is a penalty, a poster gives information, and a law forces a rule.

items.prompt: Is there an incentive to finish early?
items.passage: A company tells its workers the project is due Friday. Finishing early earns no reward, praise, or time off.
items.hint: Is anything offered to encourage the workers to finish early?
items.explanation: No. Nothing is offered for finishing early, so there is no incentive to do it. An incentive is something, like a reward, that encourages an action.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "incentive" in this sentence?
items.passage: For many students, the chance to perform onstage was a powerful incentive to practice every day.
items.hint: What did the chance to perform make the students want to do?
items.explanation: The chance to perform made students want to practice, so motivation is the closest meaning. A distraction or excuse would pull them away from practicing.

words.definition: suggested or understood without being said directly

hero.text: Nova never said she was proud of the new cadet, but her huge smile made it implicit.

words.everyday: The poem's message about loneliness is implicit; the poet shows an empty chair instead of saying it.

contrast.nonExample: A sign in the hallway says in bold letters: "NO RUNNING."
contrast.explanation: The rule is stated directly, which makes it explicit, not implicit. An implicit message is suggested without being said.

items.prompt: Is Grandma's message implicit?
items.passage: When Grandma saw muddy shoes on her clean floor, she said nothing. She just raised her eyebrows and looked at the doormat.
items.hint: Did Grandma say her message in words?
items.explanation: Yes. Grandma never said "wipe your feet," but her look made the message clear. A message understood without being said is implicit.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: The story never says the character is nervous, but it shows her hands shaking and her voice cracking. Her nervousness is ___.
items.clue: never says; shows her hands shaking
items.hint: Is the nervousness said directly, or shown through clues?
items.explanation: Explicit would mean the story says it directly. Here it is only shown through details, so it is implicit. It is not imaginary, because the clues show it is real.

items.prompt: What does "implicit" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: There was an implicit agreement among the friends: whoever arrived first saved seats for everyone.

options.text: understood without being said out loud

items.hint: Did the friends ever write or say the rule?
items.explanation: The friends all knew the seat-saving rule without anyone stating it. An agreement understood without being said is implicit. One written and signed would be explicit.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: Although the coach never stated it, the ___ message of her speech was that the team needed to work harder.
items.hint: "Never stated it" is the key clue.
items.explanation: The coach never stated it, so the message was suggested, not said: implicit. Explicit, printed, and official messages are all stated directly.

items.prompt: What is the implicit message of the ad?
items.passage: In a TV ad, a famous runner drinks a bottle of ZoomFizz and then wins a race. The ad never actually claims the drink helped her win.

options.text: that the drink will help you win

items.hint: What does the ad want you to believe without saying it?
items.explanation: The ad never claims the drink helped, but showing her win right after drinking it suggests that idea. A message suggested but not said is implicit.

words.definition: to step in to change what is happening, often to stop a problem

hero.text: When two cadets started arguing, Kai intervened and helped them talk it out calmly.

words.everyday: The lifeguard intervened when a young swimmer drifted into deep water.

contrast.nonExample: Ben watched his little brother struggle with a puzzle and let him figure it out alone.
contrast.explanation: Ben stayed out of it, so he did not intervene. To intervene is to step in and change what is happening.

items.prompt: Which person intervenes?

options.text: A teacher reads quietly at her desk.
A teacher leaves the room to get lunch.
A teacher steps between two students about to fight.
A teacher hears about a fight a week later.

items.hint: Look for someone who steps in while something is happening.
items.explanation: Stepping between two students stops the fight while it is happening. That is intervening. Hearing about it a week later is too late to change anything.

items.prompt: The prefix inter- means "between," as in international. The root ven means "come," as in convention (a coming together). When you intervene, you...

options.text: come between people or events to change what happens

items.hint: Inter- = between. Ven = come.
items.explanation: Intervene means to "come between": you step into a situation to change it, like stopping an argument.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: If the river keeps rising, the town will have to ___ by stacking sandbags along the banks.
items.hint: The town needs to step in to stop a problem.
items.explanation: Stacking sandbags is stepping in to stop a flood, which is intervening.

items.prompt: Does anyone intervene?
items.passage: A crowd watches a stray dog run toward a busy street, but no one moves to stop it.
items.hint: Does anyone step in to change what happens?
items.explanation: No. Everyone just watches, and no one steps in. To intervene, someone must act to change what is happening.

items.prompt: Which phrase is closest in meaning to "intervened" in this sentence?
items.passage: The referee intervened before the argument between the players could turn into a shoving match.
items.hint: What did the referee do before things got worse?
items.explanation: The referee stepped in to stop the argument from getting worse. Watching closely or walking away would not change what happened.

words.definition: not connected to or important for what is being discussed

hero.text: During the mission briefing, Bolt kept talking about his favorite snack, which was irrelevant to the plan.

words.everyday: In a report about volcanoes, a paragraph about your pet hamster would be irrelevant.

contrast.nonExample: In an essay about healthy eating, Kira included facts about fruits and vegetables.
contrast.explanation: Those facts connect directly to the topic, so they are relevant, not irrelevant. Irrelevant details have nothing to do with the topic.

items.prompt: What does "irrelevant" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The lawyer said the witness's comment about the weather was irrelevant to the case.
items.hint: Does the weather have anything to do with the case?
items.explanation: The weather has nothing to do with the case, so the comment is not connected to the topic. That is irrelevant. It might still be true and polite.

items.prompt: The prefix ir- means "not," as in irregular. If relevant means "connected to the topic," irrelevant means...
items.hint: Ir- = not.
items.explanation: Ir- (not) + relevant (connected to the topic) = not connected to the topic. Ir- is used in place of in- before words that start with r.

items.prompt: Is this detail irrelevant?
items.passage: In a book review of a mystery novel, Sam explains how the clues in the story build suspense.
items.hint: Does the detail connect to the topic of the review?
items.explanation: No. How the clues build suspense is directly connected to reviewing a mystery novel, so it is relevant, not irrelevant.

items.prompt: Why is the cousin's car irrelevant?
items.passage: "Your argument for a longer recess is strong," said Ms. Grant, "but the part about your cousin's new car is irrelevant. Stick to reasons about recess."

options.text: It doesn't connect to the argument about recess

items.hint: What does Ms. Grant tell the student to stick to?
items.explanation: "Stick to reasons about recess" shows the car has nothing to do with the topic. Nothing says the detail is false or too long; it just does not connect.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what irrelevant means.

chunks.text: and the key to solving the case.

items.hint: Why would a judge ignore something?
items.explanation: A judge ignores comments that are not connected to the question, so "to the question being decided" fits. If it were the key to the case, it would be very relevant.

words.definition: to give good reasons that show something is right, fair, or true

hero.text: Rex justified his choice to close the bridge by showing everyone the cracks in its supports.

words.everyday: On the math test, students had to justify their answers by showing their work.

contrast.nonExample: When the teacher asked Lucy why she picked answer B, she said, "Just because."
contrast.explanation: "Just because" gives no reasons, so Lucy did not justify her answer. To justify, you explain with reasons or evidence.

items.prompt: Does Theo justify his idea?
items.passage: Theo argues that the class pet should be a fish, explaining that fish are quiet, cheap to feed, and easy to care for.
items.hint: Does Theo give reasons?
items.explanation: Yes. Theo supports his idea with three reasons. Giving reasons that show an idea is right is justifying.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The museum had to ___ spending so much on one painting, so it explained that the painting would bring in thousands of visitors.
items.hint: The museum "explained" why the spending made sense.
items.explanation: Explaining that the painting would bring in visitors gives a good reason for the spending. That is justifying.

items.prompt: What does "justify" mean in this question?
items.passage: Can you justify your claim that some dinosaurs had feathers?

options.text: give reasons or evidence that support it
say it in a louder voice

items.hint: What would you need to show to prove your claim?
items.explanation: To justify a claim, you support it with reasons or evidence, such as fossils with feather prints. Saying it louder is not a reason.

items.prompt: Which response best JUSTIFIES the opinion "Our school should start later"?

options.text: Our school should really start later than it does now.
I really, really, truly think our school should start later.
Some schools in our state start at eight o'clock.
Studies show teens learn better with more sleep.

items.hint: Justifying means giving a reason, not just repeating the opinion.
items.explanation: Only the first choice gives a reason backed by evidence. The second and third just repeat the opinion more strongly, and the last is a fact that does not support it.

items.prompt: Which line uses "justify" correctly?

options.text: "Please justify the lamp so the room gets brighter."
"The bus broke down. Here's a note to justify why I'm late."
"She justified her running shoes right before the race."
"We justified over to the park after lunch."

items.hint: Justify means give a reason that shows something is fair or right.
items.explanation: The note gives a good reason for being late, so it justifies the lateness. The other lines use justify for actions it does not describe.

words.definition: a mistaken idea or belief, often one that many people share

hero.text: Pixel cleared up a common misconception: heroes do not need superpowers to help others.

words.everyday: It is a misconception that goldfish remember things for only three seconds; they can remember for months.

contrast.nonExample: Most people know that the sun rises in the east.
contrast.explanation: This belief is true, so it is not a misconception. A misconception is a belief that is wrong.

items.prompt: What does "misconception" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Many people have the misconception that bats are blind, but most bats can see quite well.
items.clue: but most bats can see quite well
items.hint: What does the word "but" tell you about the belief?
items.explanation: "But most bats can see quite well" shows the belief is wrong. A mistaken belief is a misconception.

items.prompt: The prefix mis- means "wrongly" or "badly," as in misspell and misbehave. A conception is an idea. So a misconception is...

options.text: an idea that is brand new

items.hint: Mis- = wrongly.
items.explanation: Mis- (wrongly) + conception (idea) = a wrong idea. Many people may share a misconception, but what makes it one is that it is wrong.

items.prompt: Is this a misconception?
items.passage: Lots of people believe lightning never strikes the same place twice, but some tall towers are hit dozens of times a year.
items.hint: Is the common belief true or false?
items.explanation: Yes. Many people believe it, but tall towers prove it wrong. A widely held belief that is false is a misconception.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Long ago, many people truly believed that the sun circled the Earth. They were not trying to fool anyone. This belief was ___.
items.clue: truly believed; not trying to fool anyone
items.hint: They "truly believed" it and were not trying to fool anyone.
items.explanation: A lie is said on purpose to fool someone, and a rumor is a story passed around without proof. People honestly believed this wrong idea, which makes it a misconception.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The science teacher began by correcting a popular ___: the idea that heavy objects always fall faster than light ones.
items.hint: Something "popular" needed "correcting." What kind of idea is it?
items.explanation: "Correcting a popular" idea tells you many people believe something wrong. That is a misconception. (In fact, without air resistance, heavy and light objects fall at the same rate.)

words.definition: based on facts, not on personal feelings or opinions; fair

hero.text: Juniper tried to stay objective when judging the race, even though her best friend was running.

words.everyday: A news report should be objective, giving the facts from all sides.

contrast.nonExample: "This is the most beautiful song ever written!" said the songwriter's proud mom.
contrast.explanation: That is a personal feeling, so it is subjective. Objective statements stick to facts that anyone could check.

items.prompt: Which statement is objective?

options.text: The bridge is the prettiest in the world.
The bridge is scary to walk across.

items.hint: Look for a fact that anyone could measure or check.
items.explanation: The bridge's length can be measured and checked, so it is objective. "Prettiest," "scary," and "should love" are personal feelings.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the judging?
items.passage: A baking-contest judge scores each cake with the same checklist and tastes them without knowing who baked them.
items.hint: Could the judge favor a friend?
items.explanation: Using the same checklist and not knowing the bakers keeps feelings out of the scores, so the judging is objective. Subjective judging would be based on personal feelings.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "objective" in this sentence?
items.passage: Scientists try to be objective, recording what they see even when it surprises them.
items.hint: Scientists record what they see, not what they hoped to see.
items.explanation: Recording what you see even when it surprises you means not letting your feelings decide. Unbiased is the closest meaning.

items.prompt: Is this referee objective?
items.passage: A referee calls more fouls against the visiting team because the home crowd is cheering so loudly.
items.hint: Is the referee basing calls on facts or on the crowd's feelings?
items.explanation: No. The referee lets the crowd influence the calls instead of judging the facts. That is biased, not objective.

items.prompt: Which sentence is objective, and why?
items.passage: Ines wrote two sentences about the rainforest. (1) "The rainforest gets over 200 centimeters of rain a year." (2) "The rainforest is the most amazing place on Earth."

options.text: Sentence 2, because it shows strong feelings
Both, because they are about the same rainforest
Sentence 1, because it states a fact that can be checked
Neither, because both sentences are short

items.hint: Which sentence could you check with measurements?
items.explanation: Rainfall can be measured, so sentence 1 is objective. "Most amazing" is a personal feeling, so sentence 2 is subjective.

words.definition: to notice or become aware of something, using your senses or your mind

hero.text: Kai could perceive the faint sound of a kitten meowing beneath the fallen boards.

words.everyday: Some animals can perceive colors that humans cannot see.

contrast.nonExample: Noah walked right past the new painting in the hallway without noticing it at all.
contrast.explanation: Noah did not notice the painting, so he did not perceive it. To perceive is to become aware of something.

items.prompt: What does "perceive" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Dogs can perceive sounds that are too high for people to hear.
items.hint: What can dogs do with sounds people cannot hear?
items.explanation: Dogs can notice sounds that people cannot. Perceive means to notice or sense something.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence.
items.passage: The change in the music was so slight that only trained ears could ___ it.
items.hint: A very slight change is hard to notice. What can trained ears do?
items.explanation: "So slight" tells you the change is hard to notice; only trained ears could perceive (notice) it.
